opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think evaluations are one of the most underrated parts of building AI. Every time we train a new model, the big question is: what can it actually do? And the honest answer is that we often don't fully know until we measure it carefully. Evals are how we turn vague impressions like "this model feels smarter" into something concrete we can track, compare, and reason about.

What excites me is that the frontier keeps moving so fast. A benchmark that seemed impossibly hard a year or two ago can get saturated surprisingly quickly, so we're constantly asking what the next meaningful test should be. Increasingly that means moving away from multiple-choice trivia toward tasks that look like real work, the kinds of things doctors, engineers, lawyers, or researchers actually spend their days on. If we want to understand how AI will affect the economy and people's lives, we need to measure performance on things that genuinely matter.

It's also important from a safety perspective. Before we release a model, we want to know whether it has capabilities that could be risky, such as helping with dangerous biology or carrying out autonomous cyberattacks. Good evals give us early warning signs, help us decide which safeguards are needed, and let us be transparent with the public about what these systems can and can't do.

So for me, evals sit at the intersection of science, product, and safety. They're how we keep ourselves honest about progress, and I think that matters more and more as these models get more capable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses measuring what models can do, but does not explain that models may have capabilities before people adopt them for those uses.

r002.rationale: It says evaluations can provide early warning signs before release, but does not connect them to detecting capabilities before widespread use would make those capabilities apparent.

r003.rationale: It notes that the frontier moves quickly, but does not argue that judging the pace of AI change requires tracking capability improvement rather than current shortcomings.

r004.rationale: It supports public transparency about model capabilities, but does not say that sharing measured progress helps society prepare for coming changes.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think evals are exciting because they're really the only honest way we have of knowing what these models can and can't do. There's so much hype and so much anecdote in this field, and someone will say "the model solved this hard problem for me" and someone else will say "it failed at something trivial," and both of those are true at the same time. Evals are how you turn that noise into something you can actually reason about.

What I find most interesting is that measuring capabilities well is genuinely hard. It's not just writing a test set. You have to ask: what does it actually mean for a model to be good at, say, software engineering, or scientific reasoning? And then you have to build something that captures that in a way that isn't gamed, isn't contaminated by training data, and still tells you something meaningful when the model gets it right. A lot of the benchmarks people quote are saturated or were never really measuring the thing people assumed they measured. So there's a constant race where the models get better and the evals have to get better too.

And then the "important" part, for me, is that evals sit at the center of basically every decision. If you want to know whether a model is safe to deploy, you need measurements. If you want to know whether it can help with biology or cyber tasks in ways that could be dangerous, you need measurements. If you want to know whether we're actually making progress toward something that can do real economically valuable work, you need measurements. Without good evals, you're flying blind, and you end up making those decisions on vibes. I'd much rather we make them on evidence. So it feels like a place where careful, somewhat unglamorous work has a really outsized effect on how the whole field moves.

astra-6.text:
What I find exciting is that you’re trying to understand what a model can actually do, and that’s surprisingly hard. You can have a conversation with it and come away impressed, but that doesn’t tell you where it’s reliable, where it struggles, or whether it can handle a task that takes many steps.

Evaluations help turn those impressions into evidence. And that matters both for making models better and for deciding how to use them responsibly. If we understand their capabilities and limitations, we can make better decisions about where they’re useful and where they still need human oversight.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find exciting is that evaluating a model forces you to make a very abstract question concrete: what can it actually do? You can have an impressive interaction with a model, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you how reliably it can solve a problem, where it needs help, or when it’s going to fail.

And that’s why evaluation is so important. If we want to use these systems in meaningful ways, we need evidence about their strengths and limitations. Good evaluations help us measure progress, identify risks, and figure out what to improve next. The really interesting part is that as models get more capable, we also have to get better at asking questions that genuinely test them.
